UPPER GI BLEED IN THE ED 
 
 
 
 
 
MANAGEMENT 
* ABC approach to initial resuscitation 
* 2 large bore IV lines à Give warm Balsol or Ringers Lactate (10mls/kg) 
* Keep NPO 
* Transfuse if: 
• Haemodynamic instability despite 1 crystalloid fluid bolus 
• Hb < 9 in a high risk patient i.e. elderly; coronary artery disease 
• Hb < 7 in a low risk patient 
• Avoid over transfusion if the bleeding may be 2° varices 
*If haemodynamically unstable à Give FFP (10-20mls/kg) 
*Pantoprazole (PantolocÒ) 
• Loading dose 80mg 
• Consider Infusion: 200mg in 200mls N/S @ 8 mls/hr 
*Consider Sengstaken-Blakemore Tube for variceal bleeds  
*Notify surgeons ASAP 
*NB – no role for TXA in UGIB 
 
HISTORY 
Symptoms 
• Abdominal pain 
• Haematemesis 
• Melena 
• Haematochezia 
• Syncope (especially in elderly) 
Risk factors 
• Alcohol abuse 
• NSAIDs 
• Antiplatelet / anticoagulant therapy 
• Previous GI bleed 
• Liver disease 
• Smoking 
DISPOSITION 
 
Discharge only if patient meets ALL criteria: 
• Stable  
• No witnessed haematemesis in ED 
• Blatchford Score = 0 
 
Discharged patients should follow up at SOPD 
 
EXAMINATION 
*	­HR ¯BP = moderate – severe blood loss 
* Digital rectal examination to assess for melena 
* Look for signs of liver disease  
* Signs of acute abdomen suggest perforation 
 
INVESTIGATIONS 
* NB! initial Hb may be normal 
* VBG, FBC, U&E, INR & Type and screen 
* LFT only if indicated 
* CXR erect à assess for free air under diaphragm 
* POCUS to assess volume status 
BLATCHFORD SCORE 
 
* Urea < 6.5 mmol/l 
* Hb > 13 (males) ; > 12 (females) 
* Systolic BP > 110 mmHg 
* Pulse < 100 bpm 
* Absence of melena, syncope, cardiac failure  
   or liver disease
